content:
If you have fallen or are worried about falling, your GP or another professional may refer you to a falls service. Arthritis can increase falls risk through pain, stiffness, weaker muscles and fear of moving.

This guide explains what a falls assessment usually involves. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Who may be referred

  • People who have fallen, especially more than once.
  • People who feel unsteady or have difficulty walking.
  • People who have had a fall with injury.
  • People who are afraid of falling.

What the assessment may include

  • Questions about previous falls and what happened.
  • Checking walking, balance and strength, for example standing from a chair.
  • Reviewing medicines that can cause dizziness or drowsiness.
  • Blood pressure, including when standing.
  • Eyesight, hearing, feet and footwear.
  • Continence and night-time toilet trips.
  • Home hazards and fear of falling.

How arthritis is taken into account

Tell staff which joints are painful and what makes pain worse. Exercises can usually be adapted. Pain relief, walking aids and footwear may also be reviewed.

How to prepare

  • Bring a list of your medicines.
  • Note when and where any falls happened.
  • Wear your usual shoes and bring walking aids, glasses and hearing aids.
  • Bring someone with you if that helps.

What may follow

You may be offered strength and balance classes, physiotherapy, an occupational therapy home visit, equipment, medicine changes or a referral for eyesight or bone health checks.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will they stop my medicines?

Changes are discussed with you. Do not stop medicines yourself.

Is exercise safe with arthritis?

Exercise is recommended for osteoarthritis, and falls programmes are adapted to you.

Living With Arthritis is an independent charity and is not part of Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). Everyone's situation is different, so follow the advice of your own GP and care team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
